claim: AKT is implicated in neurological disorders.
source: AKT is implicated in neurological disorders.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: AKT has three isoforms: AKT1/AKT2/AKT3.
source: AKT has three isoforms, AKT1/AKT2/AKT3, with brain cell type-specific expression that may differentially influence behavior.
evidence: This is established knowledge about AKT protein family structure.

claim: AKT isoforms have brain cell type-specific expression.
source: AKT has three isoforms, AKT1/AKT2/AKT3, with brain cell type-specific expression that may differentially influence behavior.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work by the authors and others.

claim: AKT isoforms may differentially influence behavior.
source: AKT has three isoforms, AKT1/AKT2/AKT3, with brain cell type-specific expression that may differentially influence behavior.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the differential expression patterns.

claim: Sex is a determinant of neuropsychiatric disorders.
source: Because sex is a determinant of these disorders but poorly understood, sex was an experimental variable in our design.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of neuropsychiatric disorders.

claim: Male Akt1 mutant mice show increased anxiety-like behavior in the open field arena test.
source: OFA testing revealed that male Akt1 KO mice spend significantly less time exploring the center compared with wild-type (WT) littermate controls (Figure 1A; t(42)=4.789, p<0.001), indicating increased anxiety-like behavior, which was not due to differences in overall movement (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Female Akt1 WT and KO mice were indistinguishable in the open field arena test.
source: In contrast, female Akt1 WT and KO mice were indistinguishable (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: No genotype effects were observed in Akt2 or Akt3 mutants for both sexes in the open field arena test.
source: No genotype effects were observed in Akt2 or Akt3 mutants for both sexes (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1A and 1B.

claim: Akt1 KO male mice show reduced open arm time in the elevated plus maze compared with controls.
source: Consistent with increased anxiety-like behavior, Akt1 mutants also displayed a male-specific reduction in open arm time compared with controls (Figure 1C; t(42)=2.156, p=0.037), which was not due to differences in distance moved (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Akt2 KO male mice show decreased open arm time in the elevated plus maze compared with WT controls.
source: EPM testing also revealed decreased open arm time in Akt2 mutant males compared with WT controls (Figure 1C; t(28)=2.651, p=0.013) that was not due to differences in overall movement (Figure 1C), indicating increased anxiety-like behavior.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Akt1 or Akt2 deletion had no effect on female mice in the elevated plus maze.
source: In contrast, Akt1 or Akt2 deletion had no effect on female mice (Figure 1D) while Akt3 deletion had no effect on either sex (Figure 1C,D) in the EPM.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1C and 1D.

claim: Akt3 deletion had no effect on either sex in the elevated plus maze.
source: In contrast, Akt1 or Akt2 deletion had no effect on female mice (Figure 1D) while Akt3 deletion had no effect on either sex (Figure 1C,D) in the EPM.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1C and 1D.

claim: Akt1 and Akt2 deficiency affect the expression of anxiety-related behaviors in a sex-specific fashion.
source: Together these OFA and EPM data demonstrate that Akt1 and Akt2 deficiency affect the expression of anxiety-related behaviors in a sex-specific fashion.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the OFA and EPM data presented.

claim: No latency differences in each training component were detected for any Akt mutants compared to WT controls in the Morris Water Maze.
source: No latency differences in each training component were detected for any Akt mutants compared to WT controls (Figure 2), indicating normal spatial learning, reversal learning, and visual acuity.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Akt1 KO males displayed reduced target platform crossings compared with controls in the Morris Water Maze probe test.
source: We found no differences in target quadrant time between Akt1 KO and WT mice (Figure 2A,B; males t(16)=1.187, p>0.05; females t(16)=-.489, p>0.05), but Akt1 KO males displayed reduced target platform crossings compared with controls (Figure 2A; t(16)=2.389, p=0.030), indicating a sex-specific deficit in more precise spatial memory.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Akt1 KO males have a sex-specific deficit in more precise spatial memory.
source: We found no differences in target quadrant time between Akt1 KO and WT mice (Figure 2A,B; males t(16)=1.187, p>0.05; females t(16)=-.489, p>0.05), but Akt1 KO males displayed reduced target platform crossings compared with controls (Figure 2A; t(16)=2.389, p=0.030), indicating a sex-specific deficit in more precise spatial memory.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the reduced platform crossings data.

claim: Probe tests revealed no differences in Akt2 KO or Akt3 KO mice in the Morris Water Maze.
source: Probe tests revealed no differences in Akt2 KO (Figure 2C,D) or Akt3 KO mice (Figure 2E,F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2C-F.

claim: There is a subtle requirement for Akt1 in males during spatial memory formation.
source: Combined, these data suggest a subtle requirement for Akt1 in males during spatial memory formation.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the Morris Water Maze data.

claim: No effects on training performance or contextual and cued LTM were found in Akt1 KO mice in fear conditioning.
source: We found no effects on training performance or contextual and cued LTM evaluated 24 hr post-training in Akt1 KO mice (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3A and 3B.

claim: Contextual LTM was impaired in Akt2 KO males but not females.
source: For Akt2 KO mice, contextual LTM was impaired relative to WT littermates in males (Figure 3C; t(28)=-2.474, p=0.020) but not females (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figures 3C and 3D.

claim: No fear conditioning effects were detected in Akt3 KO mice.
source: In Akt3 KO mice, we detected no fear conditioning effects (Figure 3E,F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3E and 3F.

claim: Akt1 KO mice showed a male-specific enhancement in extinction learning compared with WT controls.
source: Interestingly, Akt1 KO mice showed a male-specific enhancement in extinction learning compared with WT controls (Figure 4A,B; males F(1,30)=8.571, p=0.006).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figures 4A and 4B.

claim: No extinction acquisition differences were observed in Akt2 KO or Akt3 KO mice.
source: No extinction acquisition differences were observed in Akt2 KO (Figure 4C,D) or Akt3 KO (Figure 4E,F) mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 4C-F.

claim: Extinction LTM was enhanced specifically in Akt1 KO males compared with WT controls.
source: Consistent with their more rapid extinction learning, extinction LTM was enhanced specifically in Akt1 KO males compared with WT controls (Figure 4A; F(1,30)=9.121, p=0.005).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Akt1 KO male mice showed reduced renewal of extinguished fear relative to WT controls.
source: When we tested renewal of extinguished fear by re-exposing mice to the CS in the original training context, Akt1 KO male mice also showed reduced renewal relative to WT controls (Figure 4A; F(1,30)=7.187, p=0.012).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Akt2 KO males showed enhanced fear renewal compared to WT controls.
source: With Akt2 KO mice, we detected no differences in extinction LTM from WT controls (Figure 4C,D), but KO males showed enhanced fear renewal (Figure 4C; F(1,26)=5.969, p=0.022).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Akt3 KO mice showed no differences from WT controls in extinction LTM or renewal.
source: Akt3 KO mice showed no differences from WT controls in extinction LTM or renewal (Figure 4E,F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 4E and 4F.

claim: Akt1 and Akt2 play roles in associative fear memory processes of males.
source: These data support a role for Akt1 and Akt2 in associative fear memory processes of males.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the fear conditioning and extinction data.

claim: AAV expression was confirmed in both the prelimbic (PL) and infralimbic (IL) regions of the PFC.
source: We confirmed AAV expression in both the prelimbic (PL) and infralimbic (IL) regions of the PFC (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Expression of AKT1 in the PFC of Akt1 KO males is restored in neurons.
source: Furthermore, we confirmed that expression of AKT1 in the PFC of Akt1 KO males (Akt1 KO+AKT1PFC) is restored in neurons (Figure 5C), both excitatory and inhibitory neurons (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: No difference in conditioned fear learning or contextual and cued 24 hr memory was found in Akt1 KO+AKT1PFC mice compared to sham-treated WT and KO males.
source: We found no difference in conditioned fear learning or contextual and cued 24 hr memory in Akt1 KO+AKT1PFC mice compared to sham-treated WT and KO males (Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: A significant effect on extinction learning was found in the PFC AKT1 restoration experiment.
source: However, we found a significant effect on extinction learning (Figure 5E; F(2,34)=5.400, p=0.009).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Akt1 KO-sham mice showed enhanced extinction learning compared with WT-sham mice.
source: In agreement with our previous experiment (Figure 4), Akt1 KO-sham mice showed enhanced extinction learning compared with WT-sham mice (p=0.009).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Akt1 KO+AKT1PFC males showed a significant difference in extinction learning from Akt1 KO-sham mice but not from WT-sham mice.
source: Akt1 KO+AKT1PFC males showed a significant difference in extinction learning from Akt1 KO-sham mice (p=0.047) but not from WT-sham mice (p=0.875), consistent with the idea that PFC AKT1 activity underlies the extinction effects we observed in Akt1 KO mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: PFC AKT1 activity underlies the extinction effects observed in Akt1 KO mice.
source: Akt1 KO+AKT1PFC males showed a significant difference in extinction learning from Akt1 KO-sham mice (p=0.047) but not from WT-sham mice (p=0.875), consistent with the idea that PFC AKT1 activity underlies the extinction effects we observed in Akt1 KO mice.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the rescue experiment data.

claim: A significant difference in extinction LTM was found between Akt1 KO-sham and WT-sham groups.
source: We also found a significant difference in extinction LTM between Akt1 KO-sham and WT-sham groups (Figure 5E; F(2,34)=4.388, p=0.020, post-hoc comparison p=0.035) but no significant difference between WT-sham and Akt1 KO+AKT1PFC groups (post-hoc comparison p=0.985), supporting the notion that PFC-expressed AKT1 rescued Akt1 KO effects on extinction LTM.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: PFC-expressed AKT1 rescued Akt1 KO effects on extinction LTM.
source: We also found a significant difference in extinction LTM between Akt1 KO-sham and WT-sham groups (Figure 5E; F(2,34)=4.388, p=0.020, post-hoc comparison p=0.035) but no significant difference between WT-sham and Akt1 KO+AKT1PFC groups (post-hoc comparison p=0.985), supporting the notion that PFC-expressed AKT1 rescued Akt1 KO effects on extinction LTM.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the rescue experiment data.

claim: No significant difference in extinction renewal was observed between WT-sham and Akt1 KO+AKT1PFC groups.
source: Finally, we examined extinction renewal following PFC AKT1 expression. We did not observe a significant difference between WT-sham and Akt1 KO+AKT1PFC groups (Figure 5E; F(2,29)=1.018, p=0.374, post-hoc comparison p=0.605).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: AKT1-mediated PFC function underlies effects of Akt1 deficiency on the expression of extinction-related behaviors.
source: However, the combined data support that idea that AKT1-mediated PFC function underlies effects of Akt1 deficiency on the expression of extinction-related behaviors.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the PFC rescue experiment data.

claim: No differences in OFA center time were found between male Akt1 cKO and WT mice.
source: We found no differences in OFA center time (Figure 6A) or EPM open arm time (Figure 6B) between male Akt1 cKO and WT mice, suggesting AKT1 activity in forebrain excitatory neurons or late development is not required for normal anxiogenic-like responses.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: No differences in EPM open arm time were found between male Akt1 cKO and WT mice.
source: We found no differences in OFA center time (Figure 6A) or EPM open arm time (Figure 6B) between male Akt1 cKO and WT mice, suggesting AKT1 activity in forebrain excitatory neurons or late development is not required for normal anxiogenic-like responses.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: AKT1 activity in forebrain excitatory neurons or late development is not required for normal anxiogenic-like responses.
source: We found no differences in OFA center time (Figure 6A) or EPM open arm time (Figure 6B) between male Akt1 cKO and WT mice, suggesting AKT1 activity in forebrain excitatory neurons or late development is not required for normal anxiogenic-like responses.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the conditional knockout data.

claim: Akt1 cKO males performed similarly in the MWM to WT controls.
source: Additionally, Akt1 cKO males performed similarly in the MWM to WT controls (Figure 6C), suggesting AKT1 activity in forebrain excitatory neurons or late development is not required for spatial memory as well.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: AKT1 activity in forebrain excitatory neurons or late development is not required for spatial memory.
source: Additionally, Akt1 cKO males performed similarly in the MWM to WT controls (Figure 6C), suggesting AKT1 activity in forebrain excitatory neurons or late development is not required for spatial memory as well.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the conditional knockout data.

claim: Conditional Akt1 removal had no effect on associative fear learning and cued LTM.
source: Conditional Akt1 removal also had no effect on associative fear learning and cued LTM (Figure 6D) or on extinction learning and LTM (Figure 6E), although there was a trend for enhanced fear renewal (Figure 6E; F(1, 22)=3.105, p=0.092).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Conditional Akt1 removal had no effect on extinction learning and LTM.
source: Conditional Akt1 removal also had no effect on associative fear learning and cued LTM (Figure 6D) or on extinction learning and LTM (Figure 6E), although there was a trend for enhanced fear renewal (Figure 6E; F(1, 22)=3.105, p=0.092).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: There was a trend for enhanced fear renewal in Akt1 cKO mice.
source: Conditional Akt1 removal also had no effect on associative fear learning and cued LTM (Figure 6D) or on extinction learning and LTM (Figure 6E), although there was a trend for enhanced fear renewal (Figure 6E; F(1, 22)=3.105, p=0.092).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Contextual LTM was impaired in Akt1 cKO males.
source: Interestingly, contextual LTM was impaired in Akt1 cKO males (Figure 6D; t(22)=2.535, p=0.019), suggesting AKT1 activity in forebrain excitatory neurons or late development of male mice is required for contextual fear memory.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: AKT1 activity in forebrain excitatory neurons or late development of male mice is required for contextual fear memory.
source: Interestingly, contextual LTM was impaired in Akt1 cKO males (Figure 6D; t(22)=2.535, p=0.019), suggesting AKT1 activity in forebrain excitatory neurons or late development of male mice is required for contextual fear memory.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the conditional knockout data.

claim: AKT1 activity within interneurons is required for normal extinction learning.
source: Taken together with our results from restoring neuronal AKT1 expression in the PFC (Figure 5), these data suggest that AKT1 activity within interneurons is required for normal extinction learning.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on combining the PFC rescue and conditional knockout data.

claim: No performance differences in the OFA were found between Akt1 cKO Akt3 KO mice and WT controls for either sex.
source: When we assessed anxiety-like behavior in Akt1 cKO Akt3 KO mice, we found no performance differences in the OFA (Figure 7A) or EPM (Figure 7B) compared to WT controls for either sex.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: No performance differences in the EPM were found between Akt1 cKO Akt3 KO mice and WT controls for either sex.
source: When we assessed anxiety-like behavior in Akt1 cKO Akt3 KO mice, we found no performance differences in the OFA (Figure 7A) or EPM (Figure 7B) compared to WT controls for either sex.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Spatial learning was indistinguishable between Akt1 cKO Akt3 KO and WT mice for both sexes in the MWM.
source: In the MWM, spatial learning was also indistinguishable between Akt1 cKO Akt3 KO and WT mice for both sexes (Figure 7C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 7C and 7D.

claim: Akt1 cKO Akt3 KO mice showed significantly reduced target quadrant time and target platform crossings compared with WT littermates for both males and females.
source: However, Akt1 cKO Akt3 KO mice did show significantly reduced target quadrant time and target platform crossings compared with WT littermates for both males (Figure 7C; quadrant time t(20)=2.172, p=0.042; crossings t(20)=3.406, p=0.003) and females (Figure 7D; quadrant time t(22)=3.262, p=0.004; crossings t(22)=2.283, p=0.032), indicating pronounced spatial memory deficits with simultaneous Akt1 and Akt3 removal.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figures 7C and 7D.

claim: Simultaneous Akt1 and Akt3 removal causes pronounced spatial memory deficits.
source: However, Akt1 cKO Akt3 KO mice did show significantly reduced target quadrant time and target platform crossings compared with WT littermates for both males (Figure 7C; quadrant time t(20)=2.172, p=0.042; crossings t(20)=3.406, p=0.003) and females (Figure 7D; quadrant time t(22)=3.262, p=0.004; crossings t(22)=2.283, p=0.032), indicating pronounced spatial memory deficits with simultaneous Akt1 and Akt3 removal.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the double knockout data.

claim: Training performance of Akt1 cKO Akt3 KO mice was normal in associative fear conditioning.
source: Similarly in associative fear conditioning, training performance of Akt1 cKO Akt3 KO mice was normal but contextual LTM was impaired for both males (Figure 7E; t(20)=2.213, p=0.039) and females (Figure 7F; t(23)=2.250, p=0.034) compared with WT controls.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 7E and 7F.

claim: Contextual LTM was impaired in Akt1 cKO Akt3 KO mice for both males and females.
source: Similarly in associative fear conditioning, training performance of Akt1 cKO Akt3 KO mice was normal but contextual LTM was impaired for both males (Figure 7E; t(20)=2.213, p=0.039) and females (Figure 7F; t(23)=2.250, p=0.034) compared with WT controls.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figures 7E and 7F.

claim: AKT3 substitutes for AKT1 activity in female mice during spatial memory tasks.
source: Taken together with the results in single Akt isoform KO mice (Figures 2–3), these data suggest that AKT3 substitutes for AKT1 activity in female mice while AKT1 can substitute for AKT3 in both sexes during spatial memory tasks.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on comparing single and double knockout data.

claim: AKT1 can substitute for AKT3 in both sexes during spatial memory tasks.
source: Taken together with the results in single Akt isoform KO mice (Figures 2–3), these data suggest that AKT3 substitutes for AKT1 activity in female mice while AKT1 can substitute for AKT3 in both sexes during spatial memory tasks.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on comparing single and double knockout data.

claim: All three AKT isoforms play a role in contextual fear memory of male mice.
source: Furthermore, these findings suggest all three AKT isoforms play a role in contextual fear memory of male mice.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the fear conditioning data across different genotypes.

claim: Akt1 cKO Akt3 KO males and females showed deficits in cued LTM.
source: Interestingly, Akt1 cKO Akt3 KO males and females also showed deficits in cued LTM (Figure 7E,F; males F(1,20)=5.176, p=0.034; females F(1,22)=4.533, p=0.045), suggesting Akt1 and Akt3 can compensate for each other in cued fear memory in both sexes.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figures 7E and 7F.

claim: Akt1 and Akt3 can compensate for each other in cued fear memory in both sexes.
source: Interestingly, Akt1 cKO Akt3 KO males and females also showed deficits in cued LTM (Figure 7E,F; males F(1,20)=5.176, p=0.034; females F(1,22)=4.533, p=0.045), suggesting Akt1 and Akt3 can compensate for each other in cued fear memory in both sexes.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the double knockout data.

claim: AKT1 and AKT3 provide overlapping function in the brain.
source: These data strongly implicate AKT1 and AKT3 in providing overlapping function in the brain.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the double knockout data.

claim: Female behavior and memory are regulated by AKT1 activity but AKT3 can provide compensatory function in females not available in male mice.
source: Importantly, they suggest that female behavior and memory are in fact regulated by AKT1 activity but AKT3 can provide compensatory function in females not available in male mice.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the sex-specific effects observed in the double knockout data.

claim: Higher AKT2 levels were identified in the hippocampus of female mice compared to males.
source: Comparing WT males and females, we identified higher AKT2 levels in the hippocampus of female mice (Figure 8A; t(19)=3.045; p=0.007).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of western blot data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: No sex differences in protein levels were detected for AKT1, AKT3, or total AKT levels.
source: No sex differences in protein levels were detected for the other isoforms or for total AKT levels measured with a pan-AKT antibody that recognizes all AKT isoforms (Figure 8A).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: No differences in AKT1, AKT2, and total AKT activation levels were found between sexes.
source: When AKT activation was measured between the sexes using isoform-specific and pan-AKT serine 473 phosphorylation (pAKT) antibodies, we also found no differences in AKT1, AKT2, and total AKT activation levels (Figure 8A).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: Reduced total AKT levels were found in all male Akt isoform-specific mutants compared with WT controls.
source: Using the pan-AKT antibody, we found reduced total AKT levels in all male Akt isoform-specific mutants compared with WT controls (Figure 8B; Akt1 KO t(12)=3.427, p=0.005; Akt2 KO t(12)=2.282, p=0.042; Akt3 KO t(8)=11.79; p<0.0001), with the greatest reduction in Akt3 KO mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of western blot data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: The greatest reduction in total AKT levels was found in Akt3 KO mice.
source: Using the pan-AKT antibody, we found reduced total AKT levels in all male Akt isoform-specific mutants compared with WT controls (Figure 8B; Akt1 KO t(12)=3.427, p=0.005; Akt2 KO t(12)=2.282, p=0.042; Akt3 KO t(8)=11.79; p<0.0001), with the greatest reduction in Akt3 KO mice.
evidence: This is an observation from the western blot data.

claim: Increased pAKT levels were found in male Akt1 KO mice compared with WT controls.
source: Interestingly, when we examined AKT activation with the pan-pAKT antibody, we found increased pAKT levels in male Akt1 KO mice compared with WT controls (Figure 8B; t(12)=2.541, p=0.026) but no differences in Akt2 KO or Akt3 KO males (Figure 8B).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of western blot data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: No differences in pAKT levels were found in Akt2 KO or Akt3 KO males.
source: Interestingly, when we examined AKT activation with the pan-pAKT antibody, we found increased pAKT levels in male Akt1 KO mice compared with WT controls (Figure 8B; t(12)=2.541, p=0.026) but no differences in Akt2 KO or Akt3 KO males (Figure 8B).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Decreased total AKT levels were observed in female Akt isoform-specific mutants in a pattern like that found in males.
source: When we performed the same analyses in female Akt isoform-specific mutants and WT controls, we observed decreased total AKT levels in a pattern like that found in males (Figure 8C; Akt1 KO t(14)=3.507, p=0.004; Akt2 KO t(10)=2.253, p=0.048; Akt3 KO t(7)=11.77, p<0.0001).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of western blot data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: Increased pan-pAKT levels were found in female Akt1 KO mice compared with WT controls.
source: Similarly, we found increased pan-pAKT levels in female Akt1 KO mice compared with WT controls (Figure 8C; t(14)=3.456, p=0.004) and no differences in Akt2 KO or Akt3 KO females (Figure 8C).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of western blot data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: No differences in pan-pAKT levels were found in Akt2 KO or Akt3 KO females.
source: Similarly, we found increased pan-pAKT levels in female Akt1 KO mice compared with WT controls (Figure 8C; t(14)=3.456, p=0.004) and no differences in Akt2 KO or Akt3 KO females (Figure 8C).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: Similar levels of total AKT isoform expression and activation exist between sexes in response to removing one Akt isoform.
source: These data provide evidence for similar levels of total AKT isoform expression and activation between sexes in response to removing one Akt isoform.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the western blot data comparing males and females.

claim: Increased pAKT2 levels were found in both male and female Akt1 KO mice compared with WT controls.
source: Using the isoform-specific pAKT antibodies to assay AKT isoform activation, we found increased pAKT2 levels in both male and female Akt1 KO mice compared with WT controls (Figure 8D; males t(12)=2.645, p=0.021; females t(14)=2.160, p=0.049), contributing to the higher pan-pAKT levels observed in Akt1 KO mice (Figure 8B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of western blot data shown in Figure 8D.

claim: No difference in pAKT1 levels was found in Akt2 KO mice in either males or females.
source: In Akt2 KO mice, we found no difference in pAKT1 levels in either males or females (data not shown), but pAKT1 levels were significantly higher in both male and female Akt3 KO mice compared with WT controls (Figure 8E; males t(8)=3.130, p=0.014; females t(15)=3.724, p=0.002).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text but data not shown.

claim: pAKT1 levels were significantly higher in both male and female Akt3 KO mice compared with WT controls.
source: In Akt2 KO mice, we found no difference in pAKT1 levels in either males or females (data not shown), but pAKT1 levels were significantly higher in both male and female Akt3 KO mice compared with WT controls (Figure 8E; males t(8)=3.130, p=0.014; females t(15)=3.724, p=0.002).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of western blot data shown in Figure 8E.

claim: The increased pAKT1 levels may compensate for the absence of pAKT3 in Akt3 KO mice.
source: Because Akt3 KO and WT mice showed similar pan-pAKT levels (Figure 8B,C), the increased pAKT1 levels may compensate for the absence of pAKT3 in Akt3 KO mice.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the western blot data.

claim: Male and female mice respond similarly to Akt isoform deficiency by activating the other AKT isoforms.
source: These data demonstrate that male and female mice respond similarly to Akt isoform deficiency by activating the other AKT isoforms.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the western blot data.

claim: No significant differences in phosphorylated or total levels of PDK1, GSK3β, and ERK1/2 were found in the hippocampus of Akt1 KO mice for either sex.
source: Comparing Akt1 KO and WT samples, we found no significant differences in phosphorylated or total levels of the proteins examined from the hippocampus for either sex (Figure 9A,B; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figures 9A and 9B.

claim: No differences in signaling were found in the PFC of Akt1 KO males.
source: Because AKT1 loss affected extinction (Figure 4), we also examined signaling in the PFC of Akt1 KO mice but found no differences in males (Figure 9C; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 9C.

claim: Akt1 KO females showed reduced pGSK3β levels in the PFC compared with WT controls.
source: Akt1 KO females, however, showed reduced pGSK3β levels in the PFC compared with WT controls (Figure 9D; t(12)=3.567; p=0.004).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of western blot data shown in Figure 9D.

claim: No significant differences in the proteins examined were found in the hippocampus of Akt2 KO mice for either sex.
source: Comparing Akt2 KO and WT hippocampal samples, we found no significant differences in the proteins examined for either sex (Figure 9E,F; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figures 9E and 9F.

claim: Reduced pGSK3β levels were previously found in the hippocampus of Akt3 KO males compared with WT controls.
source: In the hippocampus of Akt3 KO mice, we previously found reduced pGSK3β levels in males compared with WT controls (Levenga et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: No difference in pGSK3β levels was found between Akt3 KO and WT hippocampal samples in females.
